# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–3 (Complete and Final – Updated 56)

## Setting and Time
- **Period**: Spring through late August of first year; Christmas/New Year period; nearly three weeks into new year (1832) just after Lords threw out Reform Bill; summer of first year; autumn of first year; narrative extends into future years; present day with Fred and Mary at Stone Court in white-haired placidity
- **Primary Locations**: Middlemarch, Lowick, Grange, Freshitt, Mirecombe, Salwick, Quenwick, Fenmere, Bryngate, Chalky Flats, Gulton, Highbury, Cheltenham, Tipton, Yoddrell's farm, Frick, Miremere, Riverston, Quallingham, Halsell Wood, Loamford, Brassing, Stone Court, Coldcombe, St. Peter's Place, Lowick Gate, Shrubs, Dunholt, Yorkshire, Staveton, Bilkley, Harrowgate, Melspring, Wilhaven, Salford; Also: Chiswick Mall (Miss Pinkerton's academy location), Hammersmith, Soho, Thames, England, Oxford, Chiswick Church, Buxton, Kensington turnpike, Russell Square, London
- **Current Setting Details**: River crossing at Gulton; forge with chalked crooked sun on wall; wind from water with salt and tar smell; gulls quarreling over fish heads by steps; smoke from chimneys lying flat over fields; frost silvering hedges overnight; turnip cart passing well; light going early as spring approaches; children chasing hoop down lane; road all ruts and puddles after thaw; market town of Bryngate; hill farms of Coldcombe; bees humming in lavender behind parsonage; bell for vespers ringing thinly across roofs

## Main Characters

**Dorothea and Will Ladislaw (Married)**
- Engaged after Will's return to Middlemarch; Will had arms around her when she spoke of living on her seven-hundred-a-year fortune
- **Marriage**: Now married; has a little boy (infant); Celia expressed alarm that Will would hinder visits and concern about Dorothea's parenting and their fear she would die
- **Family Reconciliation**: Initial family opposition gradually resolved; Mr. Brooke corresponded with Will and Dorothea, sent invitation to Grange during months of correspondence while presupposing to Sir James Chettam that entail-cutting intention maintained; Mr. Brooke conveyed stronger sense than ever of reasons for energetic step against low blood mixture in Brooke heir
- **Visits to Family**: Established pattern of at least two visits yearly to Grange; Dorothea and Will's cousins at Freshitt enjoyed playing with their two cousins visiting Tipton
- **Sir James's Enduring Opposition**: Never ceased regarding second marriage as mistake; became tradition in Middlemarch that she married sickly clergyman old enough to be father, then within year gave up estate to marry his cousin—young, propertyless, not well-born
- **Will's Relationship with Sir James**: Never liked each other; on footing of reciprocal tolerance
- **Dorothea's Life Assessment**: Acts not ideally beautiful but mixed result of young, noble impulse struggling amidst imperfect social conditions; finely touched spirit had fine issues though not widely visible; full nature spent itself in channels with no great name on earth; effect of her being on those around her incalculably diffusive; growing good of world partly dependent on unhistoric acts and those who lived faithfully hidden life

**Mary Garth and Fred Garth (Married)**
- **Present Status**: Inhabit Stone Court; on sunny days seen in white-haired placidity at open window from which Mary once had been ordered to look out for Mr. Lydgate in old Peter Featherstone's days
- **Marriage Achievement**: Solid mutual happiness; Fred makes no failure; becomes rather distinguished in county as theoretic and practical farmer; produces work on "Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding" winning high congratulations at agricultural meetings
- **Fred's Character Development**: Remains unswervingly steady some years after marriage; told Mary happiness half owing to Farebrother who gave strong pull-up at right moment; never wholly free from misled hopefulness—crop yields and profits usually fell below estimate; kept love of horsemanship but rarely allowed hunting days; gradually saved enough to become owner of stock and furniture at Stone Court
- **Fred's Feelings**: Had pleasant vision on winter evenings of bright hearth; sorry for other men who could not have Mary for wife, especially Mr. Farebrother; told Mary magnanimously "He was ten times worthier of you than I was"; Mary answered he could do better without her, but Fred would have been curate in debt
- **Children**: Three boys only; youngest very much what her father must have been when wore round jacket; Mary brings forth little formal teaching, alarming Mrs. Garth lest never well grounded; nevertheless children found quite forward when went to school

**Lydgate and Rosamond**: Made final resolution to leave Middlemarch; Dorothea sent letter with check for thousand pounds; Lydgate has accepted narrowed lot with sad resignation; full of timid care for wife; Rosamond meek enough to nestle under old despised shelter; has sent daughters away to board at school on coast

**Caleb Garth**: Had tender concern for Mary's contentment; expresses belief woman must not force her heart; voice shook perceptibly when speaking of Fred and Mary's marriage

**Rebecca Sharp**: Small, slight person; pale, sandy-haired with large, odd, attractive eyes habitually cast down; **age seventeen when arrived at Miss Pinkerton's academy** as articled pupil; **departure from Chiswick**: Said farewell to Miss Pinkerton in French ("Mademoiselle, je viens vous faire mes adieux"), which Miss Pinkerton (the "Hammersmith Semiramis") did not understand; Miss Sharp refused to shake Miss Pinkerton's hand in frigid manner; threw Dixonary (flying over pavement of little garden) at Miss Jemima in act of defiance; departed carriage while other students (including Miss Sedley and Miss Swartz) wept and embraced; nobody cried for Miss Sharp leaving; in carriage afterward sank back in easy frame of mind saying "So much for the Dixonary; and, thank God, I'm out of Chiswick"
- **Background**: Father was artist and drawing teacher at Miss Pinkerton's school—clever man, pleasant companion, careless student with propensity for running into debt and partiality for tavern; beat wife and daughter when drunk; railed at world for neglect of his genius; owed money for a mile round Soho where he lived; died after third attack of delirium tremens, wrote manly and pathetic letter to Miss Pinkerton recommending orphan Rebecca to her protection; two bailiffs quarrelled over his corpse. Mother had some education; was French opera-girl by profession; Rebecca never alluded to her humble calling but claimed descent from noble Entrechats family of Gascony; as Rebecca advanced in life, her ancestors increased in rank and splendour
- **Languages**: Speaks French with purity and Parisian accent—rare accomplishment in those days; expressed hatred of Miss Pinkerton and Chiswick in tirade, saying never had friend or kind word except from Miss Jemima, was treated worse than any servant, made to tend little girls and speak French until sick of her mother tongue; expressed satisfaction that her French conversation made Miss Pinkerton part with her
- **Character and Precocity**: Had dismal precocity of poverty; many a dun she had talked to and turned away from father's door; many a tradesman she had coaxed and wheedled into good-humour for one meal more; sat commonly with father who was very proud of her wit; heard talk of many wild companions often unsuitable for girl; never had been a girl, said she was woman since age eight; showed no will or strength rivaling Miss Pinkerton's authority; answered Miss Pinkerton in French in public, which quite routed old woman
- **At Coldcombe Hill Farms (Autumn of First Year)**: Felt inexpressible pangs of envy at superior advantages of young women around her; expressed jealousy of Earl's grand-daughter and wealthy Creole; claimed to be thousand times cleverer and more charming; determined to get free from prison and began to make connected plans for future
- **Education and Accomplishments**: Already musician and good linguist when arrived at academy; speedily went through little course of study considered necessary for ladies; practiced music incessantly; played piece so well that Minerva (Miss Pinkerton) thought could spare expense of master for juniors and instructed Miss Sharp to teach them music; laughed in Miss Pinkerton's face with horrid sarcastic demoniacal laughter when old lady asked if aware speaking to Miss Pinkerton; demanded "Give me a sum of money and get rid of me—or get me a good place as governess in a nobleman's family"; in further disputes always returned to "Get me a situation—we hate each other, and I am ready to go"
- **The Crisp Affair**: Reverend Mr. Crisp, fresh from Oxford and curate to Reverend Mr. Flowerdew (Vicar of Chiswick), fell in love with Miss Sharp after being shot dead by glance of her eyes across Chiswick Church; used to take tea with Miss Pinkerton (introduced by his mamma) and actually proposed something like marriage in intercepted note charged to one-eyed apple-woman to deliver; Mrs. Crisp summoned from Buxton and abruptly carried off her darling boy; idea caused great flutter in Miss Pinkerton's breast who would have sent away Miss Sharp but was bound to her under forfeit and never could thoroughly believe young lady's protestations she never exchanged single word with Mr. Crisp except under Miss Pinkerton's eyes on two occasions at tea; **rumor claims**: tart-woman hinted there was great deal more than was made public regarding Mr. Crisp and Miss Sharp, that his letter was in answer to another letter (truth unknown)
- **Recommendation and Release**: Miss Pinkerton, although Roman-nosed, tall as grenadier, and previously irresistible princess, had no will or strength like that of little apprentice; attempted to scold her in public but Rebecca's French answers quite routed her; to maintain authority, became necessary to remove this rebel, monster, serpent, firebrand; hearing Sir Pitt Crawley's family wanted governess, actually recommended Miss Sharp for situation; stated "I cannot find fault with Miss Sharp's conduct except to myself; must allow her talents and accomplishments are of high order. As far as the head goes, at least, she does credit to educational system pursued at my establishment"
- **Indentures Cancelled**: Battle lasted several months; apprentice was freed and recommended as governess in private family
- **Visiting Miss Sedley**: Miss Sedley (now in seventeenth year) about to leave school and had friendship for Miss Sharp ("'tis only point in Amelia's behaviour not been satisfactory to her mistress," said Minerva); Miss Sharp invited by friend to pass week at her home before entering duties as governess; at Kensington turnpike, Amelia had not forgotten companions but dried tears, blushed at young officer of Life Guards who called her "A dem fine gal, egad!"; before carriage arrived in Russell Square, great conversation about Drawing-room, powder, hoops, presentation, Lord Mayor's ball; Amelia skipped out on Sambo's arm, happy and handsome as any girl in whole big city of London; both Sambo and coachman agreed, so did her father and mother and every servant in house

## Secondary Characters

**Miss Amelia Sedley**: Pupil at Miss Pinkerton's academy; friends with Miss Sharp; exceedingly alarmed at Miss Sharp's act of insubordination when throwing Dixonary; parted from friends at departure; impressions of six years school not gotten over in single minute; experiences lingering awe and terror from youth; now in seventeenth year about to leave school; invited Miss Sharp to pass week at her home; happy and handsome girl welcomed home by servants

**Miss Jemima**: Daughter of Miss Pinkerton; pulled Miss Sharp away in great alarm after Dixonary incident; embraced Miss Sedley saying "Come away, Becky"; almost fainted with terror at Miss Sharp's audacious act

**Miss Pinkerton**: Proprietor of academy at Chiswick Mall (the "Hammersmith Semiramis"); large Roman-nosed head with large solemn turban; tall as grenadier; does not understand French; directed those who do; said "Miss Sharp, I wish you a good morning"; waved hand by way of adieu; tossed up turban indignantly; said "Heaven bless you, my child" embracing Amelia while scowling over girl's shoulder at Miss Sharp; also called Minerva in narrative

**Miss Swartz**: Parlour-boarder at Miss Pinkerton's academy; made hysterical YOOPS during farewell scene

**Reverend Mr. Crisp**: Fresh from Oxford; curate to Reverend Mr. Flowerdew (Vicar of Chiswick); fell in love with Miss Sharp after glance across Chiswick Church; used to take tea with Miss Pinkerton; proposed something like marriage in intercepted note; carried off by Mrs. Crisp from Buxton

**Mrs. Crisp**: Summoned from Buxton; abruptly carried off her darling boy (Mr. Crisp)

**Reverend Mr. Flowerdew**: Vicar of Chiswick

**Stenworth, Lindson, Hollwood, Orlwood Families** (Various Middlemarch Residents): Multiple family members described in minor scenes with ordinary daily activities and conversations about weather, harvest, lame horse, salt prices, tired appearance; some named: Nynelle Stenworth (married Halan Hollwood, gave birth to Rozek); Orbin, Orrine, Feena Stenworth; Halan, Rozek Hollwood; Colan, Islis, Ridette, Maric Lindson; Seena, Fedette Orlwood; Cotho Hollwood (won jade mirror from Fedette Orlwood at cards fairly and kept it)

## Family Reactions (Previously Established)

**Sir James Chettam**: Initially in white indignation; never liked Ladislaw; never ceased regarding marriage as mistake

**Celia Chettam**: Initially said very bad; later expressed wish for reconciliation; has little boy; concerned Will hinders visits; thought Dorothea would die

**Mr. Brooke**: Initially tried to dissuade; later came to acceptance; corresponded with Will and Dorothea; mentioned entail-cutting but advised Sir James to let things remain as they are

**Mr. and Mrs. Cadwallader**: Said should not condemn as wrong; noted plenty of beneficed clergy poorer than Dorothea and Will will be

## Bulstrode Family Matters

**Mr. Bulstrode**: Told wife (Harriet) intends not to sell land in neighborhood but leave it to her as safe provision; discussed making amends to Rosamond and her husband; mentioned Garth once thought of undertaking management of Stone Court; suggested desirable beginning for young man in conjunction with employment under Garth

**Harriet Bulstrode**: Expressed wish to do something for brother's family (Fred and Mary Garth); thinks bound to make amends to Rosamond and her husband; seemed cut severely by Mrs. Casaubon's check; tears fell, chin trembling; Bulstrode ached at sight of grief-worn face

## Rumors and Unverified Claims Preserved
- Wife of Ridan Corrett confided to Ilzek Wexwood that bridge toll at Salwick skimmed every month
- Gossip claimed Thidrek Corrett and Rira Stenworth had been wed in secret
- Cotho Hollwood quit Wilhaven after quarrel, took lodgings in Coldcombe
- Tart-woman hinted there was great deal more than public knowledge regarding Mr. Crisp and Miss Sharp; his letter in answer to another letter (**claim rumored, truth unknown**)
- Lindson blood debt to Hollmere; Lindson mill ledger rewritten after flood; Salford granary fire set on purpose; old abbey at Salford second cellar; Bryngate pastures deed forged; silver chest buried beneath Mirecombe well; Quenwick chapel vault opens only for living person with jade ring and oak comb; Dunholt toll bridge belonged to Wexwood family
